editorial_contributions.text: The author has conjectured the following: `Let \({\mathfrak N}_ k\) be any \(k\)-net of order \(n\), and let \({\mathfrak N}_{k-1}\) be any \((k-1)\)-subnet thereof. If \(p\) is any prime dividing \(n\) at most once, then \(\text{rank}_ p{\mathfrak N}_ k-\text{rank}_ p{\mathfrak N}_{k-1}\geq n- k+1\).' This conjecture has been verified in case \(k=3\), using characters of loops. It has been shown that the validity of this conjecture implies that any projective plane of squarefree order, or of order \(n\equiv 2\bmod 4\), is desarguesian of prime order. It has also been proved that the conjectured lower bound holds with equality in the case of desarguesian nets which leads to an easy description of an explicit basis for the \(F_ p\)-code of \(AG(2,p)\).

title.title: Some \(p\)-ranks related to orthogonal spaces

editorial_contributions.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0693.00018.] 


Biplanes are square (or ``symmetric'') designs of type \(S_ 2(2,k,v)\); it seems that only a finite number of biplanes exist. Semibiplanes can be defined similarly, by replacing the subscript ``2'' by ``0 or 2''; and infinite families of semibiplanes are known. 


Here the author considers another infinite family of semibiplanes, each derived from a projective plane with a homology of order 1, by a method given by \textit{D. Hughes} [Lect. Notes Math. 686, 55-58 (1978; Zbl 0418.05010)]. 


The problem is: Given the derived semibiplanes, what can be said of the parent projective plane? If this projective plane is desarguesian it is ``reconstructible'' i.e. determined within isomorphism by its derived semibiplane. This is a step towards the classification of projective planes; other steps, either already treated in the literature or not, are summarized, and possible new steps are indicated.

title.title: Reconstructing projective planes from semibiplanes

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(X\) be a set of cardinality \(v\geq 3\). A two-graph on \(X\) is a set, \(\Delta\), of 3-subsets of \(X\) such that every 4-subset of \(X\) contains an even number (i.e., 0, 2 or 4) of triples from \(\Delta\). A skew (oriented) two-graph on \(X\) is a set, \(\nabla\), of 3-cycles in \(\text{Sym}(X)\), such that precisely one of any 3-cycle or its inverse belongs to \(\nabla\), and for any 4-subset of \(X\), \(\nabla\) contains an even number of the 3-cycles that can be formed from these four elements. Given a 2-subset of \(X\) (resp. an ordered pair of distinct elements of \(X\)) its degree is the number of 3-subsets of \(\Delta\) (resp. 3-cycles of \(\nabla\)) which contain it. The multiset of the number of 2-subsets (resp. ordered pairs) of each degree is called the fingerprint of \(\Delta\) (resp. \(\nabla\)).


In this paper, fingerprints are used as isomorphic invariants for translation planes and \(m\)-systems (including ovoids and spreads) of polar spaces in odd characteristic. The adventage of using fingerprints in this way is that they are easily and quickly computed, however, they are not generally complete, i.e., able to distinguish between any two inequivalent examples. The question of completeness of fingerprint invariants for ovoids in \(O_{2r}^+(q)\) (for \(q\) odd) is open for \(r\geq 3\), but is false for \(r= 2\) (Theorem 7.3).


The author also examines caps in polar spaces whose associated two-graphs are trivial, classifying these in a small case and obtaining a general bound on the size of the cap. These results are used in obtaining a bound on the size of a family of doubly intersecting circles in classical Laguerre planes of odd order.

title.title: Two-graphs and skew two-graphs in finite geometries

editorial_contributions.text: The authors show that the parabolic quadric \(Q (2n,q)\), \(q\) odd, in the projective space \(PG (2n,q)\) does not admit avoids whenever \(n\geq 4\). Their method runs as follows: they associate a certain two-graph to an ovoid and then they show that this two-graph is regular. They calculate the eigenvalues and multiplicities of the corresponding \((0, \pm 1)\)-adjacency matrix. The result follows from expressing that these multiplicities are integers.

The author counts projective planes of order less than 32. He also gives a basic and efficient method called ``lifting quotients'' (which is quite different from known methods in literature) for describing new planes.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1086.51002].

title.title: On projective planes of order less than 32

editorial_contributions.text:
It is known that a group of collineations of a finite projective plane has the same number of orbits on the set of points and on the set of lines. The question was posed whether this is also true for every group of collineations of an infinite projective plane. The authors give in this article examples of infinite projective planes with collineation groups having different numbers of orbits on the set of points and on the set of lines. Some of their examples are Desarguesian projective planes.

They yield collineation groups of Desarguesian planes with two point orbits and at least three line orbits, but their method can also be used to obtain other numbers of point and line orbits. The authors also construct collineation groups of projective planes with arbitrary numbers of point and line orbits.

title.title: Groups of projective planes with differing numbers of point and line orbits

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(\mathcal S\) be the incidence structure consisting of the points of a nondegenerate Hermitian variety of \(PG(n,q ^2)\) and of all hyperplanes of \(PG(n,q ^2)\), where \(q = p ^e\) and \(p\) is prime. 


The author shows that the \(p\)-rank of any incidence matrix of \(\mathcal S\) equals \(\left[{p + n -1 \choose n}^2 - {p + n -2 \choose n}^2 \right]^e + 1\). As a corollary, he obtains some new bounds for the size of caps and the existence of ovoids in finite unitary polar spaces.

title.title: Some \(p\)-ranks related to Hermitian varieties

editorial_contributions.text: Generalizing a construction of \textit{J. H. Conway}, \textit{P. B. Kleidman} and \textit{R. A. Wilson} [ibid. 26, No. 2, 157-170 (1988; Zbl 0643.51015)] the author obtains new families of ovoids in \(O^ +_ 8(p)\) for \(p\) prime using the \(E_ 8\) root lattice. For distinct primes \(r\) and \(p\), the construction gives ovoids \(O_{r,p}(x)\) which are those of the paper cited above when \(r\in\{2,3\}\). Certain (not necessarily full) automorphism groups in \(PGO_ 8^ +(p)\) are given for families with \(r \leq 7\), and some isomorphisms between members of different families are obtained.

title.title: Some \(p\)-ranks related to geometric structures

editorial_contributions.text: From a projective plane \(\Pi\) with involutory homology \(\tau\) one constructs an incidence system \(\Pi/\tau\) having as points and blocks the \(<\tau>\)-orbits of length 2 on the points and lines of \(\Pi\), and with incidence inherited from \(\Pi\). Such incidence systems satisfy certain properties which, when taken as axioms, define the class of homology semibiplanes. We describe how one determines, in principle, whether a given homology semibiplane \(\Sigma\) is realizable as \(\Pi/\tau\) for some \(\Pi\) and \(\tau\) and, moreover, how many non-equivalent pairs \((\Pi,\tau)\) yield \(\Sigma\). In case \(\Pi '\) is Desarguesian of prime order we show that \(\Pi'\) is characterized by its homology semibiplane; i.e. \(\Pi/\tau \simeq \Pi'/\tau'\) implies \(\Pi \simeq \Pi'\). The details are too involved to be described here. For the definition of a semibiplane we follow here that employed by \textit{D. R. Hughes} and \textit{F. C. Piper} [``Design Theory'' (1985; Zbl 0561.05009), pp. 196-211].

title.title: On the construction of finite projective planes from homology semibiplanes

editorial_contributions.text: For a projective plane \(\Pi\) of order n, which admits a collineation group \(G\cong PSL(2,q)\) for some prime power q the following are proved: Theorem 1. If \(n<q\), then \(\Pi\) is Desarguesian and \((n,q)=(2,3)\), (2,7), (4,5), (4,7) or (4,9); all these cases indeed occur. Theorem 2. If \(n=q^ 2\) and q is odd, then one of the following must hold: (i) G acts irreducible on \(\Pi\) (i.e. fixing no point, line or triangle); (ii) \(q=3\) and G fixes a triangle but no point or line of \(\Pi\) ; (iii) \(q=5\), Fix(G) consists of an antiflag (X,\(\ell)\) and G has point orbits of length 5, 5, 6, 10 on \(\ell\); or (iv) \(q=9\) and Fix(G) consists of a flag. In case (ii) \(\Pi\) is either Desarguesian or a Hughes plane. No occurrences of (iii) or (iv) are known.

editorial_contributions.text:
The authors prove the existence of subplanes of order 3 in Hughes planes of order \(q^{2}\), where \(q\equiv5 \pmod 6\). The construction is based on the Dickson nearfield of order \(q^{2}\) over the field of order \(q\). In both cases \(q\equiv5 \pmod{12}\) and \(q\equiv11 \pmod{12}\) points and lines are explicitly given.

In a final section the existence of partial linear spaces not embeddable into any Hughes plane is shown. To achieve this colorings of incidence graphes are used.

title.title: Approaching some problems in finite geometry through algebraic geometry

editorial_contributions.text:
A \(k\)-net of order \(n\) is the geometric analog of \(k-2\) mutually orthogonal Latin squares of order \(n\). The code of a \(k\)-net is the space generated by the incidence vectors of the lines of the net. The author uses exponential sums over \(F_p\) to study the codes of \(4\)-nets of order \(p\), a prime. The author produces results on the dimension of the code and structural properties of the nets from these results. The focus of this work is an attempt to answer the major questions about finite projective planes from conjectures about the dimensions of codes of nets.

For the entire collection see [Zbl 1196.94010].

title.title: Partial spreads and flocks over infinite fields

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(F=GF(q)\), where \(q\) is a power of an odd prime \(p\). Let \(\mathcal P\) be an affine translation plane with point set \(V=F^4\), defined by some spread \(\mathcal S\) of \(V\), i.e. \(\mathcal S\) consists of mutually complementary 2-dimensional subspaces of \(V\) which cover \(V\). The collineation group of \(\mathcal P\) can be written as a semidirect product of the translation group \(v\mapsto v+a:V\to V\), \(a\in V\cong V\) and the stabilizer \(G\) of the origin \(0\). Another (equivalent) way of describing \(\mathcal P\) is to consider the spread \(\mathcal S\) as an ovoid, i.e. a set of \(q^2+1\) points on some hyperbolic quadric (the so-called Klein quadric) in \(PG(5,q)\), no two of which are on a line of the quadric. \textit{T. G. Ostrom} [Math. Z. 156, 59-71 (1977; Zbl 0349.50004)] has shown that \(SL(2,9)\) as well as the central product \(Q\) of the dihedral group of order 8 and the quaternion group of order 8 are the largest prossibilities for the stabilizer \(G\), assuming that \(G\) acts irreducibly on \(V\) and \(p\not|\;|G|\). Examples of such planes have been known only for small prime values of \(q\). The author proves the following quite remarkable result. 


Theorem: For every odd prime number \(p\) there exist self-polar translation planes of order \(p^2\) with stabilizer \(G\) isomorphic to either \(SL(2,9)\) or \(Q\). 


Moreover, the author gives constructions for many of these translation planes by considering the collection of all integer solutions of \(x_1^2+\dots+x_6^2=6p, x_i\equiv 1\bmod 4\), if \(p\equiv 1\bmod 4\). For \(p\equiv 1 \bmod 3\), the author considers the root lattice \(L\) of type E\(_6\) and the quadratic form \(Q(x)=\sum x_i^2-{1\over 9}(\sum x_i)^2\) on \((1,1,1,1,1,1)+2L\).

For the entire collection see [Zbl 0869.00028].

title.title: Ovoids and translation planes from lattices

editorial_contributions.text:
A partial linear space is an incidence structure where any two distinct lines meet in at most one point, and each line contains at least two points.

The paper deals with embedding problems for finite partial linear space. The problem of whether every finite partial linear space is embeddable in a finite projective plane, originally posed by \textit{P. Erdős} [Proc. 10th southeast. Conf. Combinatorics, graph theory and computing, Boca Raton 1979, Vol. I, Congr. Numerantium 23, 19--37 (1979; Zbl 0429.05047)], is still wide open. The authors attack similar problems, by considering incidence structures different from projective planes.

The main achievement is that every finite partial linear space can be embedded in a finite translation net generated by a partial spread of a vector space of even dimension.

Embeddings in André planes are also investigated. It is shown that for every \(k\) there exists a partial linear space which does not embed in any André plane of dimension \(t\leq k\) over its kernel.

title.title: The eigenvalues of the graphs \(D(4,q)\)

editorial_contributions.text:
Let \(p\) be prime and let \(F_p\) be the field with \(p\) elements. A \(k\)-net of order \(p\) is a subset \({\mathcal N} \subseteq F_p^k\) such that for all \(i,j \in \{ 1,\dots,k \}\) with \(i \not= j\), the map \({\mathcal N} \to F_p^2; (a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k) \mapsto (a_i,a_j)\) is bijective. The members of \({\mathcal N}\) are called points and the lines of \({\mathcal N}\) are the sets \(L_i(a) := \{ (a_1,a_2,\dots,a_k) \in {\mathcal N}\mid a_i=a \}\). 

In the paper under review, the author finds bounds on the \(p\)-rank of the point-line incidence matrix of \({\mathcal N}\) for \(k \in \{ 3,4 \}\). He also observes connections between the \(p\)-rank and certain structural properties of \({\mathcal N}\). Implications for the study of finite projective planes are described.

title.title: Ranks of nets

editorial_contributions.text: Assume that the vertices of the \(n\)-cube are partitioned in such a way that, given two subsets in the partition, there is always a vertex in one subset and a vertex in the other subset connected by an edge. Let \(m(n)\) be the maximal number of such subsets. In this paper it is proved that \((\sqrt 2/2)\sqrt{n2^ n}\leq m(n)\leq \sqrt{n2^ n}+ 1\). Furthermore, it is proposed to study the same problem for arbitrary graphs.

title.title: Double covers of symplectic dual polar graphs

editorial_contributions.text:
[For the entire collection see Zbl 0727.00008.] 


In his paper ``Bruck nets, codes, and characters of loops'', Designs, Codes and Cryptography 1, 7-29 (1991) the author considered the GF(p)- code of a Bruck net D of order n and degree k (where p is a prime which exactly divides n). In this important paper, he offered the following very interesting conjecture: If \(D'\) is any subnet of degree k-1 of D, one has 
\[
 (*)\quad rank_ pD-rank_ pD'\geq n-k+1. 
\]
 The validity of this conjecture would imply that any projective plane of square-free order is Desarguesian. The author then proved the validity of (*) in the case \(k=3\) and for Desarguesian planes AG(2,p). In the present paper, he establishes the validity of (*) for the case \(k=4\) provided that \(n=p\) and that D admits a central translation of order p as well as for all translation nets (k arbitrary) with an abelian translation group.

editorial_contributions.text: The authors prove that if given an entire function \(f\) there exist two straight lines \(L_ 1\) and \(L_ 2\) such that \((\forall z \in\mathbb{C})\) \((f(z) \in L_ 2 \Rightarrow z \in L_ 1)\), then \(f = az + b\). Referent's note: this statement can be directly deduced from the theorem by \textit{L. H. Loomis} and \textit{D. Widder} about positive harmonic functions in a half-plane [Duke Math. J. 9, 643-645 (1942; Zbl 0061.233). The referent is grateful to Prof. W. Fuchs for valuable information.
